newsitem.title: INDIA: Two planes nearly collide near Delhi.
newsitem.headline: Two planes nearly collide near Delhi.

text.p: Two planes carrying hundreds of passengers narrowly missed colliding near the Indian capital, two months after the world's worst mid-air accident in which 349 people died, officials said on Sunday.

The Indian Airlines plane and the Air-India Boeing 747 came within 300 metres (yards) of each other on Saturday evening as they approached New Delhi airport from Bombay, V.K. Bhalla, president of the Indian Commercial Pilots' Association, said.
Civil Aviation Minister C.M. Ibrahim was on Indian Airlines flight IC-168 when the two aircraft narrowly missed each other, Captain S.S. Panesar, director of flight safety at Indian Airlines, said.
"It was a very close shave," Bhalla told Reuters.

Ibrahim, whose ministry is in charge of air safety, visited the cockpit of the Indian Airlines aircraft during the flight, Panesar said. Ibrahim's office declined to comment, and the minister could not be reached.
On November 12, a Saudi Arabia Airlines Boeing 747 and a Kazakh Ilyushin Il-76 freighter collided about 80 km (50 miles) west of New Delhi.
There were no survivors among the 312 people aboard the Saudi jumbo and the 37 on the Kazakh plane.

Bhalla said that on Saturday evening, the Indian Airlines pilot saw Air-India flight AI-308 overtake it and then descend in front of it at about 21,000 feet (6,400 metres). The planes were southwest of Delhi en route from Bombay.
"The distance between the two was not more than 300 metres maximum," Bhalla said. The Pioneer newspaper said there were some 400 passengers on the two aircraft.
November's mid-air collision trained an unforgiving spotlight on flight safety in India, where economic growth has spurred travel but also burdened outdated security controls.
Experts were quick to criticise the nation's air traffic control system even though initial evidence suggested November's collision may have stemmed from a tragic pilot error.
A court of inquiry has been given until mid-February to report on the accident.
A multi-million-dollar plan to modernise radar and communications systems at major airports has fallen well behind schedule, authorities said.

Due to be operational six months ago, a state-of-the-art air traffic control system built by Raytheon Co of the United States has been held up by technical glitches. In November, Raytheon said the system would be ready for use very soon.
"Air misses in the Indian air space have become a regular phenomenon," Bhalla said, noting that the sophisticated radar equipment had yet to be installed.
"Only when a crash occurs do the authorities show some enthusiasm in improving the flight safety," Bhalla said.

Director general of civil aviation H.S. Khola told Reuters authorities would review the planes' black boxes and tape recordings of the conversations between the pilots and air traffic controllers before commenting on the incident.
Both Indian Airlines and Air-India are state owned. Indian Airlines is the domestic carrier, while Air-India is the international airline.
